title: Indian IT Stocks Slide Up to 3% as Strong US Jobs Data Revives Fed Rate Hike Fears
excerpt: Nifty IT index drops 2.3% to near three-year lows as robust US employment figures and Middle East oil tensions rattle markets.
body:
• The Nifty IT index dropped 2.3% on Monday to 29,995, with Infosys, LTI Mindtree, and Mphasis each falling around 3%, while TCS, HCLTech, and Wipro declined 1-2%.
  • Strong US jobs data — nonfarm payrolls rose 162,000 in August versus expectations of 56,000 — fuelled expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike in September, with traders pricing in a 57% probability.
  • Rising crude oil prices (Brent at $96.8/barrel) amid Strait of Hormuz tensions added to pressure, dragging the broader Nifty 50 down 0.5% to a six-week low of 23,779.
  • Analysts remain divided on the sector's outlook: CLSA downgraded several IT heavyweights, while Anand Rathi argues the AI deployment cycle will ultimately benefit Indian IT services firms.

Nifty IT Index Drops to Three-Year Lows

Indian IT stocks fell sharply on Monday, with the Nifty IT index dropping 2.3% to 29,995 — leading losses across all major sectors on Dalal Street. The selloff was triggered by stronger-than-expected US employment data that revived expectations of a September interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve.

Infosys, LTI Mindtree, and Mphasis led the decline, each falling approximately 3%. Tech Mahindra, OFSS, Coforge, HCL Technologies, Wipro, Persistent Systems, and TCS dropped between 1% and 2%. The broader Nifty 50 ended 0.5% lower at 23,779.15, while the BSE Sensex shed 0.5% to 76,132.81 — both at six-week lows.

Why US Jobs Data Rattled Indian IT

US nonfarm payrolls increased by 162,000 in August, nearly three times economists' expectations of a 56,000 gain, while the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%. The robust numbers signalled that the US labour market remains stronger than anticipated, diminishing hopes for an interest rate cut and instead boosting the probability of a hike.

Traders are now pricing in approximately a 57% chance of a September rate increase. Higher US rates could curb corporate technology spending, directly impacting Indian IT firms that generate a significant share of their revenue from American clients.

"Market instability with a downward bias will continue in the short term due to periodic conflicts and higher crude oil prices."

— G. Chokkalingam, Equinomics Research

Oil Prices Add to the Pressure

The IT selloff didn't happen in isolation. Brent crude futures rose 0.6% to $96.8 per barrel after the US and Iran struck vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby areas, the latest escalation in Middle East tensions that could disrupt energy supply chains and intensify global inflation fears.

The combination of higher oil prices and rising US bond yields has weighed on Indian equities for weeks. The Nifty 50 and Sensex have shed 2.7% and 2.5%, respectively, over the past four weeks.

The AI Question Looms Large

Beyond the macro headwinds, Indian IT stocks continue to grapple with structural questions about artificial intelligence's impact on the traditional services model. The sector has endured a near three-year spending recession driven by weak discretionary budgets, elongated deal cycles, H-1B headwinds, and fears that AI tools could automate legacy IT workloads.

Analysts are divided on what comes next. CLSA recently downgraded several heavyweight IT stocks, though it remains bullish on mid-tier vendors. HSBC, meanwhile, has argued that India could serve as an "anti-AI" diversifier for foreign investors spooked by sharp swings in technology-exposed markets.

Brokerage Anand Rathi offered a contrarian take in August, arguing that the AI cycle is "pivoting from building capacity to proving payback" — a transition that is inherently services-heavy and should play to Indian IT's strengths in deployment, integration, governance, and legacy modernisation.

What Investors Should Watch

For NRI investors with exposure to Indian IT — one of the most widely held sectors in diaspora portfolios — the near-term outlook hinges on two factors: the Federal Reserve's September decision and the trajectory of crude oil prices. A rate hike would likely extend the pressure on IT valuations, while any de-escalation in the Middle East could ease broader market anxiety.

The sector's longer-term thesis depends on whether Indian IT firms can successfully pivot from traditional outsourcing to AI deployment services — a transition analysts believe could expand their addressable market even as it disrupts existing revenue streams.
